chief_complaint: spasticity, painful flexor spasms, and stiff scissoring gait 1 year after stroke requiring multidisciplinary antispasmodic evaluation
hpi_details: 64F with history of a right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke 14 months ago presents for rehabilitation follow-up regarding severe muscle stiffness and painful spasms in her left arm and left leg. Reports her left elbow, wrist, and fingers are constantly clenched tightly inward toward her chest, making it impossible to clean her palm or clip her fingernails. When walking or transferring, her left leg stiffens out straight with her foot pointing downward and turning inward, causing her toes to catch. At night, experiences painful sudden muscle jerks in her left leg that wake her up.
ideas: in significant discomfort from constant tight muscle clenching and painful nighttime spasms
concerns: frustrated by caregiver difficulty opening her clenched hand to wash inside the fingers
expectations: wants muscle relaxing medications, Botox injections, and stretching braces
pmh: Right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke 14 months ago with left hemiplegia, Hypertension, Dyslipidemia

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes a multidisciplinary step-up spasticity protocol combining stretching/splinting therapy with targeted botulinum toxin chemodenervation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: spasticity, painful flexor spasms, and stiff scissoring gait 1 year after stroke requiring multidisciplinary antispasmodic evaluation

Key HPI features: 64F with history of a right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke 14 months ago presents for rehabilitation follow-up regarding severe muscle stiffness and painful spasms in her left arm and left leg. Reports her left elbow, wrist, and fingers are constantly clenched tightly inward toward her chest, making it impossible to clean her palm or clip her fingernails. When walking or transferring, her left leg stiffens out straight with her foot pointing downward and turning inward, causing her toes to catch. At night, experiences painful sudden muscle jerks in her left leg that wake her up.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 76, BP 136/82. Neurological exam reveals classic upper motor neuron spastic hemiparesis: Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) score is 3/4 over the left elbow flexors (biceps/brachialis), left wrist/finger flexors, and left ankle plantarflexors (gastrocnemius-soleus), exhibiting marked increase in muscle tone with passive movement difficult. Clonus (8 beats) elicited at the left ankle. Tendon reflexes hyperactive (4+) with sustained clonus and positive Babinski sign on left. Passive stretching reveals early fixed shortening/contracture of the left wrist flexors and Achilles tendon.
Relevant background/PMH: Right middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke 14 months ago with left hemiplegia, Hypertension, Dyslipidemia
Current medications: Amlodipine 10mg daily, Atorvastatin 40mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Parkinsonian rigidity without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe flexor contractures.
management_principles: Multidisciplinary step-up spasticity management protocol: combine daily stretching/splinting with targeted botulinum toxin chemodenervation for focal spastic muscles.

Physical and Occupational Therapy: enforce daily prolonged stretch programs, static/dynamic splinting (resting hand splint and ankle-foot orthosis to maintain neutral alignment and prevent fixed soft tissue contractures)

Focal Chemodenervation (Gold Standard for focal/segmental spasticity): perform electromyographic (EMG) and ultrasound-guided Intramuscular Botulinum Toxin Type A injections directly into the spastic target muscles (left biceps, flexor carpi radialis, flexor digitorum profundus, gastrocnemius, and posterior tibialis) to selectively block neuromuscular acetylcholine release without systemic sedation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 64F presenting with chronic post-stroke upper motor neuron syndrome manifesting severe, velocity-dependent focal spasticity, flexor synergy contracture risk, and nocturnal spasms.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 76, BP 136/82. Neurological exam reveals classic upper motor neuron spastic hemiparesis: Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS) score is 3/4 over the left elbow flexors (biceps/brachialis), left wrist/finger flexors, and left ankle plantarflexors (gastrocnemius-soleus), exhibiting marked increase in muscle tone with passive movement difficult. Clonus (8 beats) elicited at the left ankle. Tendon reflexes hyperactive (4+) with sustained clonus and positive Babinski sign on left. Passive stretching reveals early fixed shortening/contracture of the left wrist flexors and Achilles tendon.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic Post-Stroke Spastic Hemiplegia of Left Upper and Lower Extremities with Secondary Flexor Spasms and Early Joint Contractures.
reference_soap.plan: First assess and address reversible spasticity triggers, including pain, infection, constipation, skin injury, and poorly fitting equipment. Use rehabilitation-guided prolonged stretching, positioning, and appropriately fitted splints or orthoses to preserve function and skin care. For focal or function-limiting spasticity, a trained clinician may consider botulinum toxin after goal setting and muscle selection. Oral antispasmodics are reserved for selected diffuse symptoms after review of sedation, weakness, falls, and other contraindications; monitor response and functional impact.

learning_objectives: Grade upper motor neuron spasticity accurately using the Modified Ashworth Scale (MAS 0 = normal tone, 1 = slight catch/release, 2 = more marked increase through most of range but part easily moved, 3 = considerable increase with passive movement difficult, 4 = rigid in flexion/extension)
Explain the pathophysiology of velocity-dependent spasticity resulting from upper motor neuron corticospinal tract damage and loss of descending inhibitory control over gamma spinal reflex arcs

Formulate a tiered PM&R spasticity treatment ladder progressing from physical therapy stretching/splinting, oral systemic antispasmodics (Baclofen/Tizanidine), to focal chemodenervation (Botulinum Toxin A injections), and finally Intrathecal Baclofen Pump (ITB) implantation for severe refractory cases

Recognize the critical clinical distinction between dynamic spasticity (reversible muscle hypertonia responsive to Botox/Baclofen) and fixed joint contracture (permanent structural muscle/capsule shortening requiring surgical tenotomy or tendon lengthening)

teaching.one_liner: Upper motor neuron lesion following stroke causing velocity-dependent hypertonia and muscle spasms.

must_ask.say: Does your arm or leg feel tight and snap back when you try to straighten it quickly?

must_ask.objective: Functional impact on hygiene and dressing
must_ask.say: Does the stiffness interfere with washing your palm or putting on clothes?
Do you experience sudden, painful muscle spasms in your leg at night?
Are you taking medications like baclofen or have you received Botox injections?
When did your stroke occur and how has the stiffness progressed since then?
